title: Shingon
hookLine: Kukai's esoteric school: mantra, mudra and mandala

cards: A young Japanese monk arrives at a temple in the Chinese capital, a long way from home. He's come to find a teacher. The master of the place is, the story says, not well.

When the visitor is brought in, the old man smiles and says something like: I knew you were coming, and I've been waiting a long time. Then, instead of testing him for years, he begins handing over everything he knows.
The visitor is Kukai, and the story comes from Kukai's own report home. The teaching he carried back became a school: Shingon.

teach.b: Shingon means true word, the Japanese rendering of mantra. This path met Kukai before, on the pilgrim's road and on his mountain, Koyasan. Today, what he taught there.
Shingon teaches through body, speech and mind together, and calls them the three mysteries. The body forms a mudra, a gesture of the hands. The speech recites a mantra, a sacred sound.

The mind rests on a mandala, or on a single buddha pictured within it. In Shingon's teaching, these aren't three tricks for getting somewhere. They are the Buddha's own body, speech and mind meeting the practitioner's.

teach.h: A BUDDHA IN THIS VERY BODY.
teach.b: Kukai wrote an essay on becoming a buddha in this very body. Some Buddhists of his day spoke of awakening as the end of a road many lifetimes long.
Kukai's claim was bolder: when the practitioner's gestures, words and thoughts are joined with the Buddha's, awakening is possible here, in this life, in this body. Why is it called esoteric?

teach.h: PASSED ON FROM TEACHER TO STUDENT.
teach.b: In Shingon, these practices are passed on from teacher to student after the student has been prepared, the way the old master in China handed them to Kukai.
So you'll hear Shingon described from the outside, as here, more than you'll see it explained in public; the hands, the sound and the mind are learned in person.
What anyone can notice is the idea underneath: body, speech and mind aren't obstacles to awakening. In Shingon, they're the doors.

how: Shingon Buddhists practice under a teacher, joining mudras of the hands, the recitation of mantras and meditation on mandalas; deeper practices are given only after initiation.

games.q: you're a master in the Chinese capital. a young monk from Japan arrives asking to learn. what do you do?
o: test him for many years first.
send him home with a book.
begin handing over everything you know.
games.why: Kukai's own report says the master had been waiting for him, and began passing on the whole teaching.

practice: Nothing secret, just a simple gesture used in Buddhist meditation: rest one hand in the other in your lap, palms up, the thumb tips touching lightly, as if holding a sheet of paper between them.
If the thumbs press hard, you're tense; if they drift apart, you're drifting. Let the gesture tell you how the mind is doing, and come back to it each time.
